newsitem.title: USA: Another year later, deeper in debt.
newsitem.headline: Another year later, deeper in debt.

text.p: The United States, already the world's largest debtor, sank deeper into the red in 1996, according to a Commerce Department report issued Monday.

The value of foreigners' investments in the United States last year outstripped U.S. holdings abroad by a net $182.8 billion, partly because of record buying of U.S. Treasury securities by overseas investors seeking higher returns.

At year's end, the United States net international investment position -- the amount that it owed in excess of the value of its foreign holdings -- had deteriorated to $870.5 billion from $687.7 billion.

Commerce said big capital inflows from overseas investors as well as losses on foreign exchange for Americans whose overseas assets are denominated in Japanese or European currencies accounted for much of the deterioration.

The dollar appreciated sharply in value against Japanese and European currencies last year. Thus, not only did the value of foreign holdings shrink but also any interest or dividend earnings brought home were worth less when they were converted into dollars.
"The increase in the negative position (of the United States) was only partly offset by the greater price appreciation in foreign securities than in U.S. securities," the Commerce Department said.
U.S. Treasury securities were especially attractive to foreigners.

The Commerce Department said foreigners from the private sector as well as international financial institutions increased their U.S. Treasury security holdings by $141.2 billion to a total of $530.6 billion.

Among the countries that were the sources of the largest direct investments in the United States last year were Britain at $142.6 billion; Japan $118.1 billion; the Netherlands $73.8 billion and Canada $53.8 billion.

The same countries were the key targets for Americans' foreign investment, though not necessarily in the same order. The biggest investment totals last year were placed in Britain at $142.6 billion (the same amount as Britons invested in the United States); Canada $91.6 billion; the Netherlands $44.7 billion and Japan $39.6 billion.
